Overview

Abidjan as a Business Centre

Abidjan is the economic capital of Côte d'Ivoire, while Yamoussoukro has been the official political capital since 1983. The Autonomous District of Abidjan had 6,321,017 residents at the December 2021 census. Its port, reached through the Vridi Canal, is one of the largest in West Africa, a container transshipment hub and a transit route for landlocked neighbours. Much of the country's cocoa, of which Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest producer, is processed in and exported from the city. Abidjan also hosts the headquarters of the African Development Bank and the BRVM, the regional stock exchange for the West African Economic and Monetary Union. Industrial zones at Yopougon, Koumassi and Vridi host hundreds of active companies.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Abidjan because it is the gateway for trade and investment into Côte d'Ivoire and much of francophone West Africa. Cocoa buyers and lenders need to understand exporters, cooperatives and intermediaries. Shippers and insurers need assurance on forwarders, warehouse operators and transit agents. Investors in infrastructure, energy, real estate and consumer businesses need to verify owners and partners, often family groups with interests across the region. Abidjan is also where OHADA's Common Court of Justice and Arbitration sits, so it is the focus of many regional commercial disputes and enforcement efforts.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Abidjan

01

Cocoa exporter and intermediary checks

Buyers, traders and lenders in the cocoa chain deal with Abidjan exporters, warehouse operators and intermediaries of varying substance. We research ownership, directors, related companies, litigation and adverse media, helping clients assess counterparties and spot connections that could affect supply or compliance commitments.

02

Port, transit and warehouse counterparties

Goods moving through the Port of Abidjan to landlocked neighbours pass through forwarders, transit agents and warehouses. We research these counterparties' ownership, histories and links, and support inquiries after cargo losses or suspected diversion, working alongside the client's Ivorian counsel.

03

Partner vetting for investors

Investors in Ivorian infrastructure, energy, real estate and consumer businesses often partner with family groups active across West Africa. We map their corporate interests through RCCM records and regional sources, review disputes and media, and identify links to public officials relevant to anti-corruption diligence.

04

OHADA dispute and enforcement support

Abidjan hosts the Commercial Court, the CACI arbitration centre and OHADA's Common Court of Justice and Arbitration. We give counsel factual research on counterparties, their corporate networks and publicly reported assets in Côte d'Ivoire and other OHADA states to support claims and enforcement.

05

Regional financial counterparties

Companies dealing with Abidjan-based financial firms, issuers listed on the BRVM or regional groups headquartered in Plateau need to understand ownership and track record. We research shareholders, management, regulatory and court history and media coverage across the WAEMU region.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Abidjan

Commercial Court of Abidjan

Côte d'Ivoire established commercial courts in 2012, and the Commercial Court of Abidjan hears commercial and corporate disputes at first instance, with decisions due within three months. Appeals against its rulings go to a specialised commercial appellate body in Abidjan, first set up as a commercial chamber of the Court of Appeal in 2013. Its judgments are a key source on Ivorian companies' disputes and insolvency.

OHADA's Common Court in Abidjan

The Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA), established in 1998 with its seat in Abidjan, is the final court for disputes on the interpretation and application of OHADA uniform acts, in place of national supreme courts. It also administers arbitration under OHADA rules. Its decisions, accessible through legal databases, are relevant in disputes across seventeen member states. Its case law is therefore a standard reference point for corporate research.

CACI arbitration centre

The Court of Arbitration of Côte d'Ivoire (CACI), installed on 12 August 1997, was created within the Chamber of Commerce and Industry and operates from Abidjan-Plateau. It offers arbitration, mediation, expert evaluation and accelerated claim recovery. In April 2026 it held an open day and signed a partnership with the national chamber of legal advisers to promote alternative dispute resolution.

RCCM and CEPICI

Companies are registered in the Registry of Commerce and Personal Property Credit (RCCM), created under the OHADA Uniform Act on General Commercial Law, and kept at the commercial court registry for Abidjan businesses. The investment promotion centre CEPICI runs a one-stop shop for company formation. Extracts identify directors, capital and registered address; security interests are also recorded. Later changes may be filed late.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Abidjan

TDSC has no office in Abidjan and works on Abidjan matters from Nashville. We agree the purpose with the client's Ivorian counsel first, whether vetting a cocoa exporter, checking port and transit counterparties, assessing a partner or supporting an OHADA dispute, and scope research to it. Sources include RCCM extracts, Commercial Court and CCJA decisions, BRVM disclosures, French-language media and records in other WAEMU and OHADA states. We have not verified a dedicated licensing regime for private investigators in Côte d'Ivoire, so local inquiries are carried out through qualified professionals under counsel's direction, and personal data is handled in line with Law 2013-450 and the data protection authority's requirements.

TDSC has no office in Abidjan. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Abidjan: Frequently Asked Questions

Can TDSC vet an Abidjan cocoa exporter?

Yes. We research the exporter's ownership, directors, related companies, RCCM history, court cases and adverse media in Côte d'Ivoire and abroad. Findings support counterparty, financing and sourcing decisions. Questions about export licences, quality and traceability certification are for the relevant authorities and specialist auditors, and any site visits are done by qualified local professionals.

Which court handles commercial disputes in Abidjan?

The Commercial Court of Abidjan, created in 2012, hears commercial and corporate disputes at first instance, with appeals to a specialised commercial appellate body in Abidjan. Disputes on the application of OHADA uniform acts can go on to the CCJA, which also sits in Abidjan. Venue and procedure should be confirmed with Ivorian counsel.

What does an RCCM extract show?

An RCCM extract for an Ivorian company shows its legal form, registration number, registered address, capital, directors and managers, and recorded security interests. It does not always reveal ultimate owners. We combine RCCM data with court records, BRVM or regulatory disclosures where relevant, and media to build a supported picture of ownership.

Is arbitration common for Abidjan contracts?

Many contracts provide for arbitration, either at the CACI, created within the Chamber of Commerce and Industry in 1997, or under the CCJA's OHADA arbitration rules. We support counsel with factual research on counterparties, related companies and publicly reported assets in Côte d'Ivoire and other OHADA states, ahead of or during proceedings.

In which language are Abidjan records?

RCCM extracts, court judgments, CCJA decisions and most local media are in French. Some trade, shipping and finance documentation, including material from regional institutions, is in English. TDSC works with French-language sources and provides English summaries, noting where a legal translation or interpretation should be confirmed by Ivorian counsel.
